steps.say: Renal injury in civilian life is almost always blunt. More than eighty five in a hundred cases follow road crashes or falls. The kidney sits deep behind the peritoneum, so it takes real force to injure it, and liver, spleen, and rib damage often accompany the renal injury.
steps.tx: **Blunt trauma** (road crashes and falls) causes over **85% to 90%** (eighty five to ninety in a hundred) of civilian **renal trauma** (kidney injury), with motor vehicle collisions and falls as the leading etiologies. The retroperitoneal position cushions the kidney, so injury implies major force transfer with frequent associated liver, spleen, and rib injuries. Bedside extended FAST examination sorts unstable patients for theatre while stable patients travel to CT.

vis.alt: Diagrams of FAST windows and diagnostic peritoneal lavage criteria.
vis.caption: FAST windows triage blunt trauma, selecting stable patients for multiphasic CT. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Grade one and two injuries are low grade and stay non operative. Grade one is a bruise or a blood collection under the capsule with no tear. Grade two adds a contained blood collection around the kidney or a shallow surface tear under one centimetre, still with no leak of urine.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade I** (contusion without laceration) is a subcapsular hematoma or contusion with an intact capsule and no urine leak, healing with bed rest. **AAST Grade II** (minor laceration) adds a non-expanding perirenal hematoma or cortical laceration **less than 1 cm** deep, still without collecting system rupture. Both grades are managed conservatively in stable patients with haemoglobin monitoring and re-imaging only for clinical change.

rows: Contusion or subcapsular hematoma, no laceration
Non-expanding hematoma or tear under 1 cm, no urine leak
Only if the clinical course changes

steps.say: Grade three crosses the one centimetre depth line. The tear runs deeper than one centimetre into the cortex, but the collecting system holds and no urine leaks. Most such injuries still settle without surgery if the patient remains stable and the blood collection does not expand.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade III** (deep cortical laceration) extends **greater than 1 cm** deep into cortex without urinary extravasation or collecting system involvement. Depth predicts bleeding risk, so crossing 1 cm moves the injury into high-grade territory. Most Grade III injuries still settle non-operatively in stable patients, with selective angioembolisation reserved for persistent contrast blush.

steps.say: Grade four reaches the collecting system. The tear lets urine leak out, or a segmental vessel is injured with active bleeding held in by the surrounding fascia. Urine leaks alone often heal with a stent and drainage, while ongoing arterial bleeding needs selective embolisation of the bleeding branch.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade IV** (collecting system laceration) tears into the collecting system with **urinary extravasation** (urine leaking from the tear), or injures segmental arteries or veins with active bleeding contained within **Gerota fascia** (fibrous renal envelope). Stenting plus drainage heals most urinary leaks, while continued arterial bleeding requires selective renal angioembolisation. Fascial tamponade keeps many Grade IV injuries out of theatre.

rows: Extravasation, heals with stent and drainage
Segmental injury, bleeding held by Gerota fascia

steps.say: Grade five destroys the organ or its blood supply. The kidney is shattered, the hilum is torn off, or the main artery or vein clots and the organ dies. Hilar avulsion bleeds catastrophically and forces immediate exploration, while a clotted main vessel leaves a dead kidney that later needs removal.
steps.tx: **AAST Grade V** (shattered or devascularised kidney) means a completely **shattered kidney**, **hilar avulsion** (hilum torn from its vessels), or main renal artery or vein thrombosis devitalising the organ. Hilar avulsion bleeds catastrophically into the retroperitoneum and mandates immediate exploration. A thrombosed main vessel leaves a non-perfused kidney that atrophies, with delayed ischaemic hypertension sometimes forcing nephrectomy.

rows: Hilum torn off, catastrophic bleeding, explore now
Main artery or vein clot, organ dies and atrophies

steps.say: Stable patients go to multiphasic contrast CT. Arterial, nephrographic, and delayed phases are all needed, with the delayed pictures taken at ten to fifteen minutes. Only the delayed phase reveals leaking urine, which is what separates grade three from grade four.
steps.tx: **Contrast CT** (multiphasic contrast-enhanced computed tomography) is the imaging of choice in stable patients, with arterial, nephrographic, and **delayed excretory phases at 10 to 15 minutes** (ten to fifteen minutes). The delayed phase is non-negotiable because only it demonstrates urinary extravasation, telling Grade III apart from Grade IV. A blush of contrast identifies active arterial bleeding and sends the interventional radiologist to the culprit branch for embolisation.

vis.alt: CT triage guiding selective embolisation for solid organ trauma.
vis.caption: Multiphasic CT triage maps bleeding and guides selective embolisation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Exploration is reserved for bleeding that will not stop. Ongoing instability despite resuscitation, a blood collection that keeps expanding or pulsates, and hilar avulsion all mandate opening the abdomen. Stable collections are left alone, because opening the fascia releases nature's tamponade and turns a contained injury into a nephrectomy.
steps.tx: **Indications for exploration** (mandatory operative triggers) are persistent hemodynamic instability unresponsive to resuscitation, an expanding or **pulsatile hematoma** (pulsing retroperitoneal blood collection), and Grade V vascular avulsion. Stable hematomas, however large, stay undisturbed because opening Gerota fascia releases tamponade and converts contained injuries into operative nephrectomies.

rows: Tamponade works, opening it causes nephrectomy

steps.say: Vascular control comes before the fascia is opened. The surgical team occludes the main artery and vein at the aorta and inferior vena cava first, then opens the envelope around the kidney. With inflow occluded, the kidney can be inspected calmly, bleeding branches tied, and tears repaired over drainage.
steps.tx: **Vascular control** (hilar clamping before opening Gerota fascia) secures the main renal artery and vein at the aorta and IVC prior to opening **Gerota fascia** (fibrous renal envelope), significantly reducing nephrectomy rates. With inflow controlled, bleeding segmental branches are tied, collecting system tears are closed over drainage, and the kidney is salvaged whenever possible before accepting nephrectomy.

rows: Artery and vein at aorta and IVC
Open Gerota fascia with inflow clamped
Ligate branches, close collecting system over drain
Far fewer nephrectomies on the table
